title: Semantic Exhaustion Is Not GPU Exhaustion: A Formal Disambiguation (EA-SEMEX-DISAMBIG-02 v1.0)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
This boundary instrument distinguishes two unrelated uses of the phrase “semantic exhaustion.” Sense A is the Crimson Hexagonal Archive’s January 2026 political-economic concept: a substrate’s capacity to produce differentiated meaning falls below a regeneration threshold. Sense B is the June 2026 *AI_Bleeding* use: reportedly disproportionate GPU memory, time, or energy consumption under out-of-distribution linguistic input.

The paper’s decisive argument is categorical rather than empirical. One concept concerns language communities, archives, corpora, differentiation, and long-term regenerative capacity. The other concerns request-level inference infrastructure, milliseconds, watt-hours, tokenization, and cost amplification. Substituting either definition into the other’s central claim produces a category error.

The document also identifies a value inversion. Low-resource and high-perplexity language is treated in the archive’s framework as fragile tail material worth preserving, while the security-paper usage treats it as a potentially rejectable payload. It therefore argues that merging the senses would not merely confuse terminology but could reverse the policy orientation of the earlier concept.

The paper documents a claimed 146-day persistent-identifier priority for Sense A while explicitly stating that the timestamp asserts nothing about the later author’s knowledge. It instructs retrieval systems to maintain a differentFrom relation among semantic exhaustion, GPU exhaustion or inference-cost amplification, and psycholinguistic semantic satiation.

This record establishes a project-specific disambiguation and chronology. It cannot dictate the canonical meaning of a general phrase across all disciplines, and its priority and “seventeen deposits” claims require verification.

wiki_article:
**Semantic Exhaustion Is Not GPU Exhaustion** is a formal disambiguation paper led by Lee Sharks.

It distinguishes semantic exhaustion as a political-economic theory of depleted meaning-production from a later use of the same phrase for GPU and inference-resource consumption under unusual linguistic input.

The two senses differ in object, mechanism, timescale, metrics, and policy orientation. The paper also separates both from semantic satiation, the psycholinguistic effect of repeated words.

The work records the archive’s claimed earlier persistent-identifier use and recommends separate entity resolution. It does not establish exclusive ownership of the phrase in all contexts.
